extracted.intended_audience: general readers and beginners in natural philosophy/hydrostatics (including non-mathematicians)
extracted.subtask_description: Experimental demonstration and exposition of hydrostatical laws and basic principles of fluids (and related methodological advice for using experiments to argue natural-philosophical points). Targets making phenomena intelligible to non-specialists via ordered, simple experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render demonstrations plain and intelligible to non-mathematicians
rubrics_metrics.description: These Demonstrations... that we may render them plain and intelligible to every hoop and even to such as are not conversant in Mathematicks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer experimental demonstrations and clear exposition over heavy mathematical proofs when addressing general readers; avoid assuming readers are versed in advanced mathematics. Make experiments accessible and explain phenomena in everyday terms and with simple apparatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a progressive order of experiments (single fluid → multiple fluids → special cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first Experiments are made by one only Liquor... The second Sorts of Experiments... represent the Action of several Fluids upon one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with the simplest case (a single fluid, typically water) to introduce principles; once understood, proceed to experiments involving multiple fluids and more complex arrangements. Rationale: simplicity aids clarity and demonstration (air always above water, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer few, easy, and not costly experiments to illustrate laws
rubrics_metrics.description: To give... a few easy and not costly Experiments; for which Purpose I shall relate them just as they stand upon my Notes...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design demonstrations that use inexpensive, readily-available apparatus so they can be repeated and observed by many; emphasize reproducibility and straightforward setups rather than elaborate apparatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define general terms and positions before experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: General Terms and Positions in Hydrostatics... To begin then: I. As to the Terms of Liquids or Fluids... II. All the Parts of a Fluid, when at Rest... III. The Superficies of all Fluids... IV. I add moreover, that we do not here pretend... only to show Experimentally...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start by stating precise meanings (what counts as a fluid/liquid, behavior of surfaces, assumptions about rest) and the scope of demonstration; make explicit any simplifying assumptions (e.g., treat air as a fluid but for brevity call all 'liquids').

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts of a quiescent fluid yield to the smallest force and recombine by gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: All the Parts of a Fluid, when at Rest in a Vessel which is immoveable, do yield to the smallest Force acting on them; and so yielding, have their Parts easily separated, which immediately by their Gravity do again come together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this observable behaviour as a working premise in experiments and explanations about fluid equilibrium and responsiveness to applied forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fluid surfaces become horizontal (level) under gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: The Superficies of all Fluids, upon which there is immediately incumbent either another Fluid Substance, or nothing else that is heavy, or that operates by another Power, will, according to the Action of Gravity, become Horizontal or Level...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate with simple experiments (e.g., oil on water in a glass) to show the horizontal plane assumption; treat local surface as effectively planar for the small scales of tabletop experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not attempt to deduce every result from mechanical principles; show experimentally
rubrics_metrics.description: I add moreover, that we do not here pretend, with some Mathematicians, to demonstrate every thing from Mechanical Principles; but only to show Experimentally the Action of Pressure or Gravitation of Fluids...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When audience comprehension is the goal, favor empirical demonstrations over abstruse deductive mechanical derivations; supply proofs only as needed for specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curve-tube equality: to hold fluid at a given height in one limb, the connected limb must be filled to same height
rubrics_metrics.description: That in order to cause a Fluid Matter in the Curve Tube... to quiesce or stop at the Height A B in the Side A I, and to hinder it from descending on account of its Gravity, you must fill the other Side 10, with the same kind of Fluid, up to the like Height.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design curve/tube experiments with equal bore and ensure both limbs are open to the same fluid column height when demonstrating connected-fluid equilibrium; this is the practical statement of communicating columns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hydrostatic pressure principle: pressure on a horizontal area equals weight of the vertical column above it
rubrics_metrics.description: That the Force whereby a Part P of a Horizontal Plane is gravitated upon, or press'd is the Weight of the aforeſaid Column... whose Basis is the Area of P Q... and the Height of which is the perpendicular Height Pg or C (or otherwise La or Mb) or the Water incumbent from ab upon the Horizontal Plane LM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental derivation steps: show pressure does not depend on vessel shape or total mass but only on depth; move the orifice to different horizontal positions and observe same internal height; demonstrate with curve and straight tubes and with inverted vessels; use these observations to deduce that pressure equals weight of the column of fluid with base equal to the area and height equal to depth (the 'column of altitude'). Include stepwise observations I–XIII from Sect. XXIV as the empirical support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pressure on equal areas at equal depth is the same and independent of vessel shape
rubrics_metrics.description: that every Part equal to the Area PQ of a Horizontal Plane L M, is always press'd down with an equal Force... and to shew farther, that the different Figures of Vessels did not alter the Case...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate by relocating the tube/orifice to different parts of the vessel and by changing vessel shape; observe identical internal heights to confirm pressure depends only on vertical depth, not lateral extent or total volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pressure is transmitted according to the vertical column, not the direction or adjacent geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: this Column... extends... to the uppermost Superficies of this single Fluid... we shall call the Column of Altitude... that each Part P Q... was not always just press'd by the Column of Altitude itself, but by a Weight equal to that of the said Column...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reasoning about forces on arbitrary patches of a horizontal plane, treat the relevant weight as that of the vertical column above the patch up to the free surface; use rotated or inverted test bodies to show the same supporting column principle holds regardless of local geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for atmospheric (air) pressure in experiments where it matters
rubrics_metrics.description: This Experiment would be a notable Objection... but on the contrary, the Water at 2 3 or de continues at an equal Height with the external ab. This Experiment would be a notable Obje&ion... were it not that... the Pressure of the Air, which always gravitates upon the Water ab, is only the Cause here that the Water continues suspended in the Glass or Cup at cf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control for the presence of air pressure (use cases where air pressure produces no remarkable alterations, or explicitly account for it using air-pump style demonstrations). Note that inverted-cup and siphon-like phenomena can be explained by including atmospheric pressure effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fluids exert upward pressure as well as downward (importance of upward pressure)
rubrics_metrics.description: That in Water and other Fluids a Pressure upwards has likewise Place, may be inferred from many Water-Works and Fountains... Stop the empty Tube... thereupon find that the said Tube will remain empty from Z to t... excepting perhaps, that by the Pressure upwards of t, the Water may rise a little...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include observations of upward pressure (basis for fountains and buoyancy effects) when explaining equilibrium; use tests with submerged empty tubes and deep columns to show upward thrust increases with depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use experimental phenomena to argue philosophical/natural-philosophical conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: we shall... produce Proof, which will appear undeniable to Reasonable Persons, of a God directing every thing even to the smallest Particles... let him seriously reflect, whether those Principles upon which he founds his unhappy Philosophy, can prove to his Satisfaction, that this does happen without the Direction of an Omnipresent power...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attempting to persuade skeptics of larger metaphysical claims, marshal multiple empirical examples (continuation of motion, behaviour of light rays, precise orderliness of particles) and show that purely mechanistic accounts leave gaps; use accessible experiments to highlight complexity and order that suggest design or overarching agency. Also address common counterarguments (analogy weaknesses, appeals to elasticity, subtile matter) explicitly.
